eras.title: Part 1: 1066, The Norman Conquest & Feudal Control (1066–1086)
Part 3: The Black Death & The Peasants’ Revolt (1348–1381)

milestones.title: Death of Edward the Confessor & The Three Rival Claimants
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did William of Normandy win the Battle of Hastings in 1066?
milestones.imageCaption: Bayeux Tapestry Scene 1 (c. 1070s, Musée de la Tapisserie de Bayeux): King Edward the Confessor enthroned in council with Harold Godwinson before the January 1066 succession crisis.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Rival Invasions of 1066, Stamford Bridge & The Battle of Hastings (Sept–Oct 1066).
milestones.catalyst: On **5 January 1066**, **King Edward the Confessor** died childless after twenty-four years on the throne, ending the direct Wessex line and creating an immediate royal power vacuum.
milestones.turningPoint: Within twenty-four hours, the Anglo-Saxon **Witan** elected England’s wealthiest nobleman, **Harold Godwinson**, as King Harold II, despite rival claims from **Duke William of Normandy** and Viking King **Harald Hardrada**.
milestones.impact: William secured **Pope Alexander II’s** papal banner by claiming Harold had broken a **1064 sacred oath** on relics, forcing England to prepare for a deadly two-front invasion.
milestones.bridgeToNext: With Viking longships gathering in Norway and Norman boats massing across the Channel, the first invasion struck Yorkshire in September 1066.
keyAgents: William the Conqueror (Duke William of Normandy)

keyTerms.definition: The formal legal order in which a person inherits a royal crown or throne.
The council of Anglo-Saxon nobles and churchmen who elected the king.

milestones.title: Harold’s Forced March & Victory at Stamford Bridge
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did William of Normandy win the Battle of Hastings in 1066?
milestones.imageCaption: Silver penny of King Harold II minted in London (1066, Yorkshire Museum), proclaiming his sovereign authority as King of the English during the invasion crisis.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Hardrada’s 300-ship landing in Yorkshire, Harold’s 190-mile forced march north, and his 250-mile return march south.
milestones.catalyst: In September 1066, Norwegian King **Harald Hardrada** landed **300 Viking longships** along the Yorkshire coast, threatening to tear northern England away from King Harold’s rule.
milestones.turningPoint: Marching his army **190 miles north** from London in just four days, Harold caught the Vikings completely unawares at **Stamford Bridge** on 25 September and killed Hardrada.
milestones.impact: Only **24 longships** were needed to carry the surviving Vikings home, yet the victory battered Harold’s elite **housecarls** just two days before Duke William landed unopposed at **Pevensey Bay**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Refusing to rest his exhausted warriors, Harold immediately force-marched 250 miles back south to confront William on Senlac Hill.

keyTerms.definition: A well-trained, professional Anglo-Saxon warrior armed with a heavy two-handed battleaxe.
The part-time Anglo-Saxon peasant militia called up to fight in national emergencies.

milestones.title: Senlac Hill, Feigned Retreats & Norman Victory at Hastings
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did William of Normandy win the Battle of Hastings in 1066?
milestones.imageCaption: Bayeux Tapestry Scene 52 (c. 1070s): Mail-clad Norman cavalry knights charge uphill into King Harold’s tightly locked Anglo-Saxon shield wall on Senlac Hill.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Duke William’s landing at Pevensey Bay and triumph over Harold’s shield wall on Senlac Hill near Hastings (14 October 1066).
milestones.catalyst: On the morning of **14 October 1066**, Harold locked his housecarls and peasant **fyrd** into a dense **shield wall** atop Senlac Hill, repelling Norman cavalry charges for over five hours.
milestones.turningPoint: Turning panic on his Breton flank into a trap, **Duke William** ordered repeated **feigned retreats** that lured undisciplined Saxon fyrdmen downhill onto open ground where cavalry cut them down.
milestones.impact: With the shield wall broken and Norman archers shooting high into the ranks, **King Harold was killed** and Anglo-Saxon rule ended when William was crowned on **Christmas Day 1066**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Winning one battle did not secure the kingdom: fewer than 10,000 Normans now had to control two million hostile Anglo-Saxons.
keyAgents: William the Conqueror (Duke William of Normandy)

keyTerms.definition: A deliberate military trick where soldiers fake panic and run away to lure enemies out of formation.
A well-trained, professional Anglo-Saxon warrior armed with a heavy two-handed battleaxe.

milestones.title: William’s Motte-and-Bailey Castle Blitz & Stone Keeps
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did fewer than 10,000 Normans control two million Anglo-Saxons?
milestones.imageCaption: Bayeux Tapestry Scene 45 (c. 1070s): Forced Anglo-Saxon labourers dig the steep earth motte and timber palisade of William’s castle at Hastings.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Norman Conquest, Castles, The Harrying of the North & The Domesday Book (1066–1086).
milestones.catalyst: Crowned King William I in December 1066, William led an invading elite of just **10,000 Normans** surrounded by roughly **two million** angry conquered Anglo-Saxons.
milestones.turningPoint: Using forced English labour, the Normans threw up over **500 motte-and-bailey castles** in just eight to fourteen days each, later replacing timber towers with giant **stone keeps** like Portchester.
milestones.impact: High earthen mottes and armoured garrisons let tiny groups of Norman knights guard river crossings, crush local revolts rapidly, and dominate English towns.
milestones.bridgeToNext: When wooden forts failed to stop a major rebellion at York in 1069, William unleashed merciless state terror across the North.
keyAgents: William the Conqueror (Duke William of Normandy)

keyTerms.definition: An early Norman timber fortress with a raised earth mound (motte) and palisaded courtyard (bailey).
A trusted Norman governor appointed by the king to garrison and command a fortress.

milestones.title: Scorched-Earth Terror: The Harrying of the North
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did fewer than 10,000 Normans control two million Anglo-Saxons?
milestones.imageCaption: Folio from the Peterborough Chronicle (Bodleian Library MS Laud Misc. 636), recording the starvation and devastation inflicted on northern England in 1069–1070.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Scorched-earth devastation across Yorkshire and the northern shires during the winter of 1069–1070.
milestones.catalyst: In winter **1069**, northern English rebels joined Danish allies to storm **York** and slaughter the Norman castle garrison, challenging William’s grip on the kingdom.
milestones.turningPoint: Marching north in fury, **William I** ordered the **Harrying of the North**: cavalry burned crops, slaughtered livestock, smashed ploughs, and salted farmland across Yorkshire.
milestones.impact: Chronicler **Orderic Vitalis** recorded that over **100,000 people** starved to death in the man-made famine, permanently breaking northern England’s ability to rebel.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Having crushed armed resistance by sword and castle, William next sought complete financial and legal control over every English manor.
keyAgents: William the Conqueror (Duke William of Normandy)

keyTerms.definition: The systematic burning of crops, destruction of villages, and slaughter of livestock to exterminate resistance.
The act of bringing a conquered population under total, permanent military and political control.

milestones.title: The Great Domesday Book Audit & Feudal Land Transfer
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did fewer than 10,000 Normans control two million Anglo-Saxons?
milestones.imageCaption: Folio from Great Domesday (1086, The National Archives E 31/2/2), recording landholders, plough teams, mills, and tax values across every English shire.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Nationwide shire circuits of the 1085–1086 Domesday Book tax and feudal land survey.
milestones.catalyst: Fearing a Danish Viking invasion at **Midwinter 1085**, King William met his council at Gloucester and ordered an exhaustive survey of England’s taxable wealth.
milestones.turningPoint: Royal commissioners rode into every shire to compile the **1086 Domesday Book**, counting every manor, mill, ox, and pig under strict sworn oaths.
milestones.impact: Domesday proved Anglo-Saxon thegns had been stripped of land and replaced by roughly **200 Norman barons**, locking England into a strict **feudal pyramid** under the Crown.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Although Norman kings mastered the barons, one mighty rival institution still stood beyond royal law: the Catholic Church.
keyAgents: William the Conqueror (Duke William of Normandy)

keyTerms.definition: The comprehensive land and property audit ordered by William I in 1086 to assess national taxable wealth.
The act of bringing a conquered population under total, permanent military and political control.

milestones.title: Henry II Appoints Becket & Becket’s Spiritual Transformation
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did the quarrel between Henry II and Becket end in murder?
milestones.imageCaption: The Becket Leaves (c. 1220–1240, British Library Loan MS 88): King Henry II confronts his former friend and Chancellor, Archbishop Thomas Becket.
milestones.catalyst: Energetic Plantagenet ruler **King Henry II** wanted to bring England’s wealthy Church under royal authority by appointing his loyal friend and Chancellor, **Thomas Becket**, as Archbishop.
milestones.turningPoint: Consecrated **Archbishop of Canterbury** in **June 1162**, Becket shocked the king by resigning as Chancellor, casting off silk robes, wearing a lice-ridden **goat hairshirt**, and serving Pope Alexander III.
milestones.impact: Henry’s plan for an obedient royal puppet collapsed overnight, turning his closest hunting companion into an unbending defender of Church independence.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Within two years, King and Archbishop collided head-on over whether criminal priests should face royal gallows or lenient Church courts.

keyTerms.definition: The legal system of the Catholic Church governing clergy conduct and spiritual matters.
The legal right of educated churchmen to be tried in lenient Church courts rather than royal courts.

milestones.title: The Constitutions of Clarendon & Criminous Clerks Dispute
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did the quarrel between Henry II and Becket end in murder?
milestones.imageCaption: The Becket Leaves (c. 1220–1240, British Library): King Henry II banishing Thomas Becket’s relatives into exile as the Clarendon legal crisis deepened.
milestones.catalyst: Anyone able to read a Latin psalm could claim **benefit of clergy**, allowing **criminous clerks** accused of murder or robbery to escape royal hanging in lenient Church courts.
milestones.turningPoint: In **January 1164**, Henry II issued the **Constitutions of Clarendon**, demanding that guilty clergymen be stripped of holy orders and punished by the King’s secular judges.
milestones.impact: Becket furiously refused to seal the document and fled into a bitter **six-year French exile**, while Henry confiscated Canterbury revenues and banished Becket’s kin.
milestones.bridgeToNext: When Becket returned in December 1170 and excommunicated royalist bishops, Henry’s furious outburst sparked bloodshed in Canterbury.

keyTerms.definition: A medieval clergyman accused of committing serious secular crimes like murder, theft, or rape.
A 1164 set of 16 royal customs issued by Henry II to bring Church courts under royal supervision.

milestones.title: Murder in Canterbury Cathedral & Henry II’s Barefoot Penance
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did the quarrel between Henry II and Becket end in murder?
milestones.imageCaption: Limoges enamel reliquary châsse of St Thomas Becket (c. 1190–1200): Four Norman knights strike down Becket before the altar of Canterbury Cathedral on 29 December 1170.
milestones.catalyst: Hearing that Becket had excommunicated bishops loyal to the Crown, **Henry II** raged at his court in Normandy against the turbulent priest defying his rule.
milestones.turningPoint: Four knights rode to **Canterbury Cathedral** on **29 December 1170** and hacked **Thomas Becket** to death at the altar, horrifying Christian Europe and making Becket a canonised saint.
milestones.impact: Facing rebellion and papal anger, Henry walked **barefoot through Canterbury in July 1174** to be whipped by **eighty monks**, leaving Church courts protected for centuries.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Under Henry’s youngest son King John, disastrous foreign wars and crushing taxes provoked a wider revolt from England’s barons.

keyTerms.definition: The suffering of death as a penalty for refusing to renounce religious beliefs or Church independence.
The legal system of the Catholic Church governing clergy conduct and spiritual matters.

milestones.title: ‘Softsword’, Loss of Normandy & The Five-Year Papal Interdict
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Was Magna Carta a victory for liberty or a barons’ power grab?
milestones.imageCaption: King John Offering His Crown to Papal Legate Pandulf (1563 woodcut): In May 1213, John surrendered England as a papal fief to end Pope Innocent III’s 1208 Interdict.
milestones.catalyst: Mocked as **‘John Softsword’** after losing **Normandy** to France in **1204**, **King John** squeezed English barons with punitive taxes and feuded with **Pope Innocent III** over Stephen Langton.
milestones.turningPoint: In **1208**, Innocent III placed England under a five-year **Papal Interdict**—locking churches and silencing bells—and excommunicated John in 1209 while John seized **£100,000** in Church wealth.
milestones.impact: Fearing a French invasion, John knelt in **1213** to surrender England as a **papal fiefdom** paying 1,000 marks yearly, alienating both clergy and heavily taxed barons.
milestones.bridgeToNext: John poured his extorted treasure into one huge continental gamble to win back Normandy in the summer of 1214.

keyTerms.definition: A papal decree closing all churches in a kingdom, banning church bells, weddings, and Christian burials.
A compulsory cash payment made by feudal barons to the king instead of providing knights for war.

milestones.title: Defeat at Bouvines & Rebel Barons Capture London
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Was Magna Carta a victory for liberty or a barons’ power grab?
milestones.imageCaption: Horace Vernet, The Battle of Bouvines, 27 July 1214: French King Philip II crushes King John’s allied army in Flanders, triggering baronial rebellion in England.
milestones.catalyst: In **July 1214**, French forces smashed King John’s expensive mercenary coalition at the **Battle of Bouvines** in Flanders, ending all hope of reconquering Normandy.
milestones.turningPoint: When a bankrupt John demanded yet another **scutage** tax from nobles who had refused to fight, rebel barons under **Robert Fitzwalter** renounced homage and seized **London** in May 1215.
milestones.impact: Deprived of his capital city, military prestige, and treasury, King John was cornered and forced to negotiate terms with his armed barons.
milestones.bridgeToNext: On 15 June 1215, King John rode out to the Thames water-meadow of Runnymede to seal the rebels’ sixty-three demands.

keyTerms.definition: A compulsory cash payment made by feudal barons to the king instead of providing knights for war.
The foundational principle that every person, including the monarch and government, is subject to the law.

milestones.title: Magna Carta Sealed at Runnymede & The First Barons’ War
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Was Magna Carta a victory for liberty or a barons’ power grab?
milestones.imageCaption: Original 15 June 1215 parchment exemplar of Magna Carta (British Library Cotton MS Augustus II.106), recording Clause 39 placing the King beneath the law.
milestones.catalyst: Confronted by armed barons and Archbishop Stephen Langton at **Runnymede** on **15 June 1215**, King John affixed the Great Seal to the 63 clauses of **Magna Carta**.
milestones.turningPoint: **Clause 39** ruled that no **free man** could be seized or imprisoned without lawful judgment, though **Pope Innocent III** soon annulled the charter and sparked the **First Barons’ War**.
milestones.impact: After French Prince Louis invaded and John died in **October 1216**, regent **William Marshal** reissued Magna Carta for young Henry III, cementing the **rule of law** over English monarchs.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Magna Carta protected only free men, not unfree serfs—until a catastrophic plague in 1348 transformed peasant power across England.

keyTerms.definition: The "Great Charter" of 63 clauses agreed by King John in 1215, placing royal power under the rule of law.
The ancient legal principle that a person cannot be detained indefinitely without trial or lawful cause.

milestones.title: Arrival of the Black Death & The Rural Labour Revolution
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the Black Death spark the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381?
milestones.imageCaption: Citizens of Tournai Burying Victims of the Black Death (1349, Bibliothèque royale de Belgique): Mass plague mortality emptied English manors and created a severe labour shortage.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Arrival of the Black Death at Melcombe Regis (1348) & The Peasants’ Revolt marches on London (1381).
milestones.catalyst: In **June 1348**, merchant ships from Gascony brought plague-infected fleas into **Melcombe Regis** (Weymouth), unleashing the **Black Death** across England.
milestones.turningPoint: Within two years, bubonic plague killed **35% to 50%** of England’s population, leaving silent villages, mass burial trenches, and unharvested wheat rotting in manor fields.
milestones.impact: Desperate landowners had to compete for scarce farm workers, giving surviving **peasants and serfs** the power to demand **double wages** or leave harsh feudal estates.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Alarmed by rising peasant wages and lost control, England’s noble-dominated Parliament passed harsh laws to force workers back down.

keyTerms.definition: The study of population size, density, distribution, and mortality shifts over time.
The hereditary legal bondage of peasants tied to a lord’s manorial estate.

milestones.title: The 1351 Statute of Labourers & The 1381 Poll Tax Spark
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the Black Death spark the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381?
milestones.imageCaption: Froissart’s Chroniques (c. 1470): Radical priest John Ball preaching equality to rebel crowds at Blackheath during the 1381 uprising.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Essex and Kent Poll Tax marches from Brentwood, Maidstone, and Blackheath into London (May–June 1381).
milestones.catalyst: Parliament passed the **1351 Statute of Labourers** freezing wages at pre-plague levels and **1363 Sumptuary Laws** banning commoners from wearing fine cloth or fur.
milestones.turningPoint: To fund the costly **Hundred Years’ War**, the Crown levied a third flat **Poll Tax of 12 pence** per adult in 1381; on **30 May**, Essex villagers chased tax collector **John Bampton** out of Brentwood.
milestones.impact: Thirty years of anger boiled over as thousands of Essex and Kent rebels marched on London behind **Wat Tyler** and radical preacher **John Ball**.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Storming London and burning hated tax rolls, 30,000 rebels came face to face with fourteen-year-old King Richard II at Smithfield.

keyTerms.definition: A 1351 royal law freezing agricultural wages at pre-plague rates and punishing mobile workers.
A flat tax levied equally on every individual person over fourteen regardless of income.

milestones.title: Showdown at Smithfield, Wat Tyler’s Death & End of Serfdom
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How did the Black Death spark the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381?
milestones.imageCaption: Jean Froissart, Chroniques (British Library Royal MS 18 E I): Mayor William Walworth strikes down Wat Tyler at Smithfield while young King Richard II rides out to calm the rebels.
milestones.mapCaption: Reference Map: Rebel convergence on Mile End, the Tower of London, and Smithfield (13–15 June 1381).
milestones.catalyst: By mid-June 1381, over **30,000 armed rebels** held London, storming the Tower and demanding an end to **serfdom** and unfair feudal taxes.
milestones.turningPoint: At **Smithfield** on **15 June 1381**, London Mayor William Walworth fatally stabbed **Wat Tyler**, while fourteen-year-old **King Richard II** rode forward promising freedom charters to disperse the bowmen.
milestones.impact: Although Richard broke his promises and executed John Ball, Parliament abandoned Poll Taxes and **feudal serfdom** steadily withered away across fifteenth-century England.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Lasting Legacy: Between 1066 and 1381, Magna Carta limited royal tyranny from above while peasant resistance eroded feudal serfdom from below.

keyTerms.definition: A violent, organized uprising by citizens against established government authority.
The hereditary legal bondage of peasants tied to a lord’s manorial estate.
